Thank you for submitting your article "Size control of the inner ear via hydraulic feedback" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by Didier Stainier as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal her identity: Ksenia Gnedeva (Reviewer #3).

The Reviewing Editor has highlighted the concerns that require revision and/or responses, and we have included the separate reviews below for your consideration. If you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact us.

Summary:

This paper examines the potential role of pressure in regulating the volume of the otic vesicle during zebrafish development. The authors present several lines of evidence that there is indeed transepithelial pressure: the shapes of adjacent epithelial cells are perturbed, the vesicle deflates when punctured and, using a clever device, they present some direct measurements of transepithelial pressures (values on the order of 100 Pa). They calculate, based on the geometry, the flux of fluid into the vesicle, which is fairly constant over the developmental times that they are studying. After puncturing the vesicle, the luminal volume "catches up" through an increase in the flux; they conclude that the pressure is inhibiting the flux, establishing a feedback loop.

Major concerns:

The reviewers have noted that the pressure measurements themselves are very noisy, and their reproducibility is unclear. These features make it difficult to judge the extent to which the very plausible theoretical model is or is not quantitatively consistent with the measurements. They have requested clarification on a number of aspects of the pressure measurements themselves, and asked if the connection between the theory and data can be made more precise than the mostly correlative comparison described in the paper.

Additionally, the reviewers have suggested that further analysis is warranted in order to solidify the claim that there is a causative connection between changes in hydrostatic pressure and changes in the rate of cell growth, cell proliferation, and/or cell cycle length. They have also asked about the connection between tissue-level tension and cell proliferation, the role of elasticity of the surrounding tissues, and the possibility of measuring that elasticity directly.

Separate reviews (please respond to each point):

Reviewer #1:

This is a very interesting paper on the problem of organ size regulation. It combines an impressive set of imaging and in vivo measurements with a simple mathematical model to paint a clear picture of a plausible mechanism at work the zebrafish. The logic of the analysis is very clear, as is the presentation.

Having said the above, I find that the manuscript falls short on two major fronts. First, if Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D are a general indication of the repeatability of the pressure measurements in vivo, then it is not clear to this reviewer the extent to which truly quantitative conclusions about the system can be inferred. The authors have not included any discussion about the potential sources of the large fluctuations seen in these experiments and their variability from one experiment to the next. The case for publication in eLife would be substantially enhanced if the reliability of the measurements were quantified and understood more deeply.

A second major issue concerns the connection between the eminently plausible theory presented in the paper and the quantitative observations. The verbal discussion in the paper regarding a whole range of qualitative observations dovetails nicely with what would be expected from the theory, but yet the paper does not appear to have a single graph in which a quantitative prediction of the theory is compared against experiment. The case for publication in eLife would be much stronger if such a comparison were possible. Can the authors show that there is more than a qualitative relationship between the two?

Minor Comments:

As a minor comment I would urge the authors to move the essential aspects of the presentation of the theory into the Results section. The mathematics is very straightforward and it would increase readability to have it interspersed within the Results section where appropriate.

Reviewer #2:

This paper examines the potential role of pressure in regulating the volume of the otic vesicle during the zebrafish development. The authors present several lines of evidence that there is indeed transepithelial pressure: the shapes of adjacent epithelial cells are perturbed, the vesicle deflates when punctured and, using a clever device, they present some direct measurements of transepithelial pressures (values on the order of 100 Pa). They calculate, based on the geometry, the flux of fluid into the vesicle, which is fairly constant over the developmental times that they are studying. After puncturing the vesicle, the luminal volume "catches up" through an increase in the flux; they conclude that the pressure is inhibiting the flux, establishing a feedback loop.

I think that the most interesting aspect of the manuscript is the pressure measurements. All the rest is indirect and based on correlations: the pressure feedback model is a plausible explanation for the observed morphological changes. Without the pressure measurements, this is not be an eLife paper.

However, the pressure measurements themselves are poorly developed and not convincing. There are many technical aspects that are not addressed, and many controls that need to be done.

1) Are the pressure measurements themselves dependent on the ionic composition and/or electrical potential? This is potentially important as the endolymph has an unusual ionic concentration and voltage, at least in adults. Is the high potassium concentration established at these early times?

2) Does the pressure measurement depend on the diameter of the capillary. I am surprised and concerned by the wide range of diameters (2-20 microns).

i) Is there a problem with damage – does the capillary tend to puncture the vesicle like the puncture needle. If not, why not? No details are given about the puncture needle: an "unclipped glass needle", whatever that is. What is the diameter?

ii) Is there a problem with mixing of the deionized water in the capillary with the endolymph? I would expect the diffusive exchange of fluid to be large, especially with 20 micron diameter capillaries. It looks like the total volume of the capillary is much larger than the vesicle, so the endolymph will be greatly diluted, unless the ion pumps can keep up. How long is mixing expected to take.

3) There simply are not enough measurements of pressure to be convincing, given the variabilities of the individual measurements in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

4) Figure 3—figure supplement 1 shows only a small part of the time traces. What is happening before time zero. For me to be convinced, I would like to see the whole time course starting with the capillary in the (undefined) Dannieau (sic) buffer, then the penetration of the skin, followed by the epithelium and finally entry into the vesicle lumen. How often does this experiment work? Have the recordings in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 been cherry-picked?

5) A key experiment will be to measure the pressure while puncturing and showing that it goes down (and perhaps recovers).

In summary. The most novel aspect of this paper is the pressure measurement. However, this is much too preliminary to be included in the current work. I suggest taking them out and submitting the manuscript to another journal. I do not believe that such a manuscript meets the level of conceptual advance for an eLife paper: the arguments are correlative and the model is only at the level of plausibility. In other words, the results in this manuscript are suggestive of a pressure-flux feedback model, which therefore remains a hypothesis. I encourage the authors to develop the pressure measurements, but there is a long way to go.

Reviewer #3:

The manuscript by Mosaliganti et al. investigates the mechanism of organ size control in the developing otic vesicle in zebrafish. In particular, the authors demonstrate that fluid transport into the otic vesicle results in stress and stretching of the otic epithelium, and claim that constitutes the major driving force in lumen expansion and organ growth. The authors also suggest that buildup of the pressure in the otocyst inhibits further fluid transport, thus repressing growth. Such a negative feedback mechanism can explain the observed robustness of the otic vesicle growth, and explain a catch-up growth phenomenon that they observe after puncturing the otocyst.

The authors characterize the vesicle's size using unbiased quantitative measurements, including direct measurements of the luminal pressure. Ouabain and morpholino experiments convincingly demonstrate the involvement of Na+-K+-Cl transporter, Slc12a2, in the fluid flux into the vesicle. Overall, the article is well written and beautifully illustrated. The experiments are easy to follow. All the numerical comparisons are accompanied by adequate statistical analysis. However, I believe the following concerns should be addressed in order to support the proposed conclusions.

Major concerns:

I do not entirely agree with the author's definition of growth. Organ growth is determined by an increase in tissue mass (via increase in cell number, cell size, or both). To be precise, otic vesicle growth, characterized in Figure 1F, is represented by the green curve (otic tissue volume), and not the blue curve (otic vesicle volume). Increase in the vesicle's lumen, especially after the puncture experiments, should not be called growth, if tissue volume does not change in these experiments. I, however, agree with the overall idea that hydrostatic pressure can be a driving force for tissue growth, as it may cause tissue stretching and cell proliferation, however, this is not characterized in the manuscript. In this regard, the effect of hydrostatic pressure on the rate of cell growth and proliferation, not on the changes in lumen volume, should be characterized. This should be done for all their experiments, especially for normal development and Slc12a2 morpholino experiments. It will be critical to demonstrate that there is a causative connection between changes in hydrostatic pressure, and changes in the rate of cell growth, cell proliferation, and/or cell cycle length. These data are already present in the time-lapse videos provided by the authors, and should be extracted/analyzed, as it is critical to link hydrostatic pressure to organ growth control mechanisms discussed by the authors in the Introduction of the manuscript.

– One of the concerns I have with the manuscript is that the authors seem to conclude that growth rate in the organ is determined by an equilibrium between hydrostatic pressure, regulated by fluid flux into the vesicle, and tension in the otic epithelium. Biologically, such an assumption is unlikely, as an increase in epithelial tension is a well-described trigger for cell proliferation and growth. Gudipaty et al., 2017 and Elosegui-Artola et al., 2017 are just a couple of recent articles on the matter. Authors do not consider the elastic forces exerted by the tissues surrounding the otic vesicle (e.g. mesenchyme, brain, and skin). In addition to the otic tissue viscoelastic properties, these forces are very likely to counteract the hydrolytic pressure in the vesicle, and to affect its growth. In fact, such a mechanism of growth control was recently shown to take place in the vestibular sensory organ in mice. This should be accounted for in the theoretical model proposed by the authors and mentioned in the discussion.

– Related to the previous comment, the authors estimate effective viscosity of the otic vesicle tissue from their theoretical model. To test this prediction, and to confirm the accuracy of the model, Young's modulus of the tissue should be measured directly (e.g via atomic force microscopy). Also in this context, the authors claim that puncturing perturbations (to eliminate pressure forces) allowed them to measure spatial differences in cell viscoelasticity. These experiments only suggested the local differences in tissue viscosity, direct measurements of cell stiffness should be done to confirm this suggestion.

– It is not apparent to me that the authors demonstrate clearly the causality of spatial differences in cell viscoelasticity. Again, although hydrostatic pressure sensed by all the cells in the vesicle should be the same, the local difference in the opposing elastic forces from surrounding tissues can create differential thinning of the vesicle's wall; this in turn may result in actomyosin skeleton remodeling and stiffness changes, rather than vice versa.

– In the section "tissue material properties are patterned through actomyosin regulation" the authors talk about WT and transgenic animals, without explaining what transgenes are used. It made it hard to review this section.

I'd like to disclose that as a biologist with limited biophysics background, I cannot fully review the mathematical aspects of the work, and trust that one of the other reviewers has the expertise necessary to judge the accuracy of the theoretical model proposed here.

Minor Comments:

– To test their model's predictions, the authors conduct puncture experiments to evaluate the role of hydrolytic pressure on the growth rate of the otic vesicle. Although the authors demonstrate that punctures heal fast relative to the growth rate of the organ, such manipulations are invasive and are not fully sufficient to support their conclusions. Direct manipulation of the chemi-osmotic potential, for example, could be done to change the rate of endolymph accumulation, and to test its effect on organ growth. This could be achieved by injecting hydrophilic inert compounds, such as ficoll, into the otic vesicle or into the tissue surrounding it. If water transport across an epithelium is, in fact, the main driving force for otic vesicle growth, increasing osmolality of the endolymph should induce accelerated growth and increase cell proliferation rates.

results.result: The zebrafish otic vesicle develops through distinct morphological stages from 12-45 hpf, including placode formation (12 hpf), mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (14-16 hpf), cavitation (16-24 hpf), and rapid growth (16-45 hpf), ultimately forming a closed ovoid epithelial structure filled with endolymph.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 provide a comprehensive developmental timeline supported by confocal imaging data (Figure 1A-D) with clear temporal staging. The morphological transitions are well-documented through imaging evidence, and the description of the final structure is consistent with established inner ear anatomy.

results.result: During otic vesicle growth (16-45 hpf), cell number increases three-fold while average cell size decreases, resulting in constant tissue volume until 28 hpf. The majority (77%) of vesicle size increase is due to lumen volume expansion rather than tissue growth (23%).
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C10 present quantitative morphometric data from n=10 embryos with standard deviations reported (Figure 1E-F). The measurements are internally consistent and the mathematical relationship between cell number, cell size, and tissue volume is logically sound. The finding that lumen expansion dominates growth is a key observation supported by direct volumetric measurements.

results.result: Epithelial thickness decreases from 20 μm to 4 μm in lateral and medial regions during growth, with lumenal surface area growth being linear over time. Cell stretching contributes more to surface area growth early (≤33 hpf) while cell proliferation dominates later (>33 hpf).
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C42-C44 are supported by quantitative imaging data (Figure 1H, Figure 6D) showing temporal dynamics of epithelial thinning and surface area expansion. The identification of a 33 hpf transition point where proliferation exceeds stretching is based on direct measurements and provides mechanistic insight into growth regulation.

results.result: Mitotic cells fail to round fully in regions where the otic epithelium contacts the hindbrain and ectoderm, with division planes aligned to the surface normal. This alignment increases over developmental time as cells stretch, and the growing vesicle deforms adjacent hindbrain and skin tissues.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C16 are supported by observational and quantitative data from confocal microscopy (Figure 2A-J) with n=54 mitotic cells analyzed and statistical significance reported (p<1.0e-4). The correlation between cell stretching and division plane alignment is consistent with mechanical stress-driven spindle orientation observed in other systems (cited prior work). The deformation of adjacent tissues provides independent evidence for pressure development.

results.result: Lumenal pressure in the otic vesicle increases from 100 Pa at 30 hpf to over 300 Pa at 48 hpf, measured using a novel piezo-resistive pressure probe. These values are similar to measurements in adult guinea pig inner ears.
results.evaluation: Claim C17 is supported by direct pressure measurements using a validated probe (Figure 3C-D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) with measurements from 5-9 embryos per timepoint and statistical significance (p<0.05). The probe calibration and validation are thoroughly documented. Claim C18 appropriately contextualizes the findings with prior literature, though the comparison across species and developmental stages should be interpreted cautiously.

results.result: Puncturing the otic vesicle causes immediate volume loss (30-40%), epithelial thickening, and cell shape changes from squamous to columnar while preserving cell volume. These experiments demonstrate that lumenal fluid is under hydrostatic pressure, pressure generates epithelial stress that stretches cells, and the tissue exhibits viscoelastic behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C23 are supported by experimental data from puncture experiments (Figure 3E-H) with n=10 embryos and statistical significance reported. The immediate elastic response (thickening) and long-term viscous response (irreversible deformation over developmental time) provide strong evidence for viscoelastic tissue properties. The preservation of cell volume during shape change is an important control demonstrating mechanical rather than osmotic effects.

results.result: A hydraulic negative feedback loop exists between pressure and fluid transport for size control: the vesicle adjusts endolymph flux in response to pressure perturbations, with pressure negatively regulating fluid flux.
results.evaluation: Claims C25, C56, and C30 integrate mathematical modeling predictions (Equation 9-13) with experimental validation from puncture-regeneration experiments (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The linear correlation between fluid flux and volume asymmetry (Figure 4H) supports the model prediction. However, the molecular mechanism linking pressure to flux regulation is not fully elucidated, though ion pump experiments (C31-C34) provide supporting evidence.

results.result: The otic epithelium rapidly seals within 5 minutes after puncture, and punctured vesicles completely regenerate lumenal volume through increased growth rate (catch-up growth) to restore bilateral symmetry. Fluid flux correlates with volume difference between left and right vesicles.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C27, C29 are supported by dye injection experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D) and time-lapse imaging of regeneration (Figure 4B-H) with n=10 embryos. The demonstration of catch-up growth is a key finding that enables testing of the feedback model. The correlation between flux and volume asymmetry (Figure 4H) provides quantitative support for the regulatory mechanism.

results.result: Ion pumps are required for lumenal expansion: ouabain (Na+-K+-ATPase inhibitor) causes dose-dependent decreases in vesicle volume and completely inhibits growth and regeneration at 500 μM. Morpholino knockdown of Na+-K+-ATPase and blockers of chloride channels also inhibit fluid transport. Growth is sensitive to extracellular pH.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C34 are supported by pharmacological and genetic perturbation experiments (Figure 5A-F) with appropriate controls and dose-response relationships. The ouabain results are consistent with prior work (Hoijman et al., 2015). However, the experiments do not fully distinguish between direct effects on ion transport versus indirect effects on cell health or epithelial integrity. The n=5 sample size for some experiments is relatively small.

results.result: The effective viscosity of otic vesicle tissue is 6.3±0.30×10^6 Pa·s from 24-36 hpf and 2.2±0.13×10^7 Pa·s from 36-48 hpf, indicating the tissue becomes more viscous through development.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C37 are supported by calculations from the mathematical model using measured pressure, geometry, and growth rate data (Equation 1). Error propagation is properly calculated and reported. The values are within the range of experimentally measured tissue viscosities (Gordon et al., 1972). However, the model assumes spherical geometry and uniform properties, which are approximations of the actual vesicle structure.

results.result: Cells retain columnar shapes independent of tissue curvature, suggesting material property patterning rather than geometry drives differential strain. Cell stretching plays a more significant role in early growth while proliferation is more important in later stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C38 and C41 are supported by cell tracking data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B) and analysis of surface area contributions (Figure 6D). The observation that cell shape is independent of curvature argues against Laplace's law as the primary determinant of regional differences. The temporal transition in growth mechanisms is quantitatively demonstrated.

results.result: F-actin and Myosin II are apically localized prior to lumenization (12-16 hpf), undergo non-uniform changes during early growth (16-22 hpf), and relocalize to apicolateral junctions by 30 hpf. Cell deformation during normal growth and after puncture correlates with actomyosin localization, suggesting actomyosin tension sets tissue elasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C50 are supported by transgenic reporter imaging (Figure 6E-J) with n=22 cells analyzed for correlations. The temporal dynamics of actomyosin localization are well-documented. The linear correlation between deformation and actomyosin levels (Figure 6I-J) supports the mechanical role. However, correlation does not prove causation, and the directionality of the relationship (does actomyosin cause stiffness or does stiffness recruit actomyosin?) is not definitively established.

results.result: Cytochalasin D treatment decreases apical myosin fluorescence, increases secretion rates (2-5X), and causes preferential expansion in the dorsoventral diameter. Spatial patterning of actomyosin can produce spatially varied strain in response to uniform pressure.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 are supported by drug perturbation experiments (Figure 6K-M) with n=12-16 embryos. The correlation between myosin loss and increased flux (Figure 6L) and the anisotropic expansion (Figure 6M) support the model that actomyosin patterning modulates pressure-driven strain. However, cytochalasin D has pleiotropic effects on actin dynamics, and the interpretation that reduced elasticity causes increased flux requires the assumption that the feedback mechanism remains intact.

results.result: Hydrostatic lumenal pressure develops in response to fluid transport across the otic epithelium to drive growth. Sustained cell thinning is caused by in-plane epithelial tension in response to lumenal pressure. Transepithelial fluid flow is the primary source of lumen fluid accumulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C55, C59, C60 represent integrative conclusions supported by multiple lines of evidence: direct pressure measurements (C17), puncture experiments (C19-C23), ion pump requirements (C31-C34), and volumetric analysis (C10). The inference that transepithelial flow is the primary source (C60) is supported by the observation that lumen volume exceeds tissue volume (Figure 1F), though alternative sources are not exhaustively ruled out.

results.result: The negative feedback architecture is similar to the chalone model in that growth feeds back to inhibit growth rate, but pressure-based feedback allows nearly instant communication via hydraulic coupling compared to diffusion-limited morphogen strategies.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58 appropriately contextualize the findings within existing theoretical frameworks. The comparison to chalone models is conceptually valid, and the advantage of hydraulic coupling over diffusion is physically sound. However, the claim of 'nearly instant' communication is qualitative and not quantitatively validated. The actual timescales of pressure equilibration and feedback response are not measured.

results.result: Fluid pressure is postulated to be a fundamental regulator of developmental growth in lumenized organs, with hydraulic feedback giving rise to robust size control. Hydraulic interactions are relevant to many internal organs with vesicular and tubular origins.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 are explicitly stated as postulates and represent extrapolations beyond the zebrafish otic vesicle data. While the otic vesicle results are well-supported, the generalization to all lumenized organs requires validation in other systems. Claim C63 cites recent work (Chan et al., 2019) supporting relevance to mammalian embryos, but the universality of the mechanism remains to be established.

results.result: Pressure homeostasis mechanisms may vary across organs and developmental stages. In the inner ear, pressure is initially regulated by feedback between pressure and fluid flux, but later development requires a physical pressure relief valve.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 are supported by the current study (C65) and prior work from the same group (Swinburne et al., 2018, C66). The temporal transition in regulatory mechanisms is an important insight. However, the molecular identity of the early feedback mechanism linking pressure to flux is not fully elucidated in the current work.

results.result: Fluid accumulation is a feature of developmental growth for several lumenized organs (brain, eye, gut, Kupffer's vesicle, inner ear, mammalian embryo), driven by water transport across epithelia. For brain and eye, fluid accumulation coincides with increased hydrostatic pressure. Specific ion transporters necessary for fluid accumulation have been identified.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C70 represent established knowledge from prior literature with appropriate citations. These claims provide important context for the current work but are not novel findings of this study. The citations appear appropriate and the statements accurately represent the cited work.

results.result: Catch-up growth is a developmental phenomenon where organs transiently elevate growth rate after perturbation. Examples include fly imaginal discs (ecdysone signaling), vertebrate organ transplants, and bone growth (insulin signaling).
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74 represent established knowledge from prior literature with appropriate citations. These claims provide important conceptual context for the catch-up growth experiments in the otic vesicle but are not novel findings. The definition (C71) is clear and the examples are well-documented in the cited literature.

results.result: Dysregulation of pressure homeostasis causes diseases including hypertension, Ménière's disease, glaucoma, and hydrocephalus. The otic vesicle is wedged between hindbrain and skin and is surrounded by extracellular matrix, mesenchymal cells, skin, and brain.
results.evaluation: Claim C75 represents general medical knowledge appropriately stated. Claims C76-C77 are observational facts supported by imaging data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G-H). These claims provide important anatomical context for understanding the mechanical environment of the developing otic vesicle.

results.result: Prior work identified Na+-K+-ATPase activity in chick otic vesicle as setting up transmural potential for water and ion movement. In zebrafish, the Na+-K+-Cl− transporter Slc12a2 is defective in little ear mutants, supporting a role for ion pumps in ear growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 accurately represent prior literature (Represa et al., 1986; Abbas and Whitfield, 2009) and provide important context for the ion pump experiments in the current study. The citations are appropriate and the statements correctly summarize the cited work.
